title: Online Learning
description: The lesson that runs reading straight into writing: three remarks by e-learners, printed under a line that names who spoke, where and when, and settles nothing else - because a quotation is evidence of an opinion and never proof of a fact; the disagreement between them, two saying the time is not saved and one reporting the students who expect e-learning to be easier because there is no journey to make, and the exact place that reasoning breaks, the saved minutes having been spent getting to the course and never on it; the hedge if not more and what it adds to a claim; the time commitment as hours of the week promised to one thing and therefore to nothing else; making more time read properly - not a twenty-fifth hour added to a day but hours already going somewhere sent somewhere else, which is why sleeping less works and hoping, counting or postponing do not; the flexibility John Bears claims for distance learning, the freedom of the hour and the freedom of the place, and the sharpest point of the page, that flexibility answers when and where while the commitment answers how many, so that the two never contradict each other and an objection about time counters nothing; the benefits and the drawbacks of studying that way, ending on the freedom that lets the work happen and equally lets it stop; then the comma with exactly two jobs - fencing a phrase in apposition, an explanation added to the noun it follows, with a comma at each end and not one, the sentence having to stand when the phrase is lifted out, and additional never meaning useless since the grammar survives the removal and the claim does not; and separating the items of a list, both jobs meeting in a single sentence; and finally the formal argumentative letter to a man never met - formal English for the one reason that he is a stranger, a view actually stated, arguments that give the reader something he can check rather than insistence, restatement or a head count, and the tactful counter that grants the point and sets something beside it without taking the grant back
sources: Official programme transcript - .claude/skills/content-ecole-tn/references/programmes-officiels/programme/bac-math/anglais.md, Unit 2 "EDUCATION MATTERS" UNIT OUTLINE (p. 87, lesson 4: Reading quotations / Writing - Punctuation, Commas in apposition, Writing a formal argumentative letter / Expressing opinion / no pronunciation focus) and Unit 2 lesson 4 "On-line Learning" (p. 101-102)

Pupil's Book - SKILLS For LIFE, Fourth Year Secondary Education, CNP Tunisia 241403P00, Unit 2 lesson 4 "On-line Learning", p. 101-102 (the three quotations by e-learners taken from the ESL magazine of June 2003 and the activity asking the class whether it agrees with them, the completion task on the third of them, the "Using commas" activity on the two commas of that quotation and on the phrase following the name of John Bears, the quotation from John Bears on the flexibility of distance learning p. 102, the DEVELOP YOUR WRITING SKILL task asking for a formal letter stating benefits or drawbacks, and the printed comma rule and WHAT I CAN DO NOW boxes; the lesson prints no MY NEW WORDS and no MY GRAMMAR box)

Teacher's Book - SKILLS For LIFE, CNP Tunisia 641404, KEY of Unit 2 lesson 4 (p. 25) - re-solved before use: the guide gives NO closed key for this lesson. It states that the completion task "would foster several alternative options for making more time" and is to be pooled by the class, so the criterion used here (an option moves hours that were already committed elsewhere, which is what the printed example of sleeping less does) is a reading of that instruction and not a transcribed answer; it explains that the reading activity leads into the use of commas when adding a phrase to another as an explanation and points at the two commas around a three-word phrase in the third quotation; and for the letter it asks only that the writing process be followed and that peer correction be used
